summary: Look at a system from two distances: how its services fit together and how one service works inside.
goals: How contracts connect the two levels
How to move through a design session

steps.title: One system, two levels of detail
body: Consider a food-delivery app. From far away, it has a few services—Orders, Couriers, and Payments—with their own data. They communicate through an API gateway and events. Up close, each box is a program with classes, database tables, and rules. These are high-level design (HLD) and low-level design (LLD).
steps.callout: Neither level is more real. They answer different questions for different readers and change at different speeds.

steps.title: High-level design is the map
body: HLD decides what the main parts are and how they connect: which services exist, what data each owns, how they communicate, and what happens when traffic grows or a component fails. The course so far has mostly worked at this level. Its main output is a diagram with the reasons for each choice.
steps.callout: A useful HLD can fit on one page. Detailed explanations of one box belong in that component’s LLD.

steps.title: Explain the trade-offs in the map
body: Placing an order should not wait for a courier to be found, so Orders publishes an event for Couriers to process later. Payments needs transactions, so it uses a relational database. Courier locations change every few seconds and create tens of thousands of writes each second, so they use a fast key–value store that can overwrite old locations. Each choice follows from the data and workload.
steps.callout: Every connection and data store on an HLD diagram is a choice with alternatives. Be ready to explain what the choice gives up.

steps.title: Low-level design opens one box
body: Now zoom into the Orders service. LLD decides how that component is built: its modules or classes, the interfaces between them, its database tables and indexes, its algorithms, and how it handles errors. A controller accepts HTTP requests, an order service applies business rules, a repository talks to the database, and a client calls Payments.
steps.callout: Small interfaces around databases and other services make the main logic easier to test. See Testing.

steps.title: Define states, data, and edge cases
body: An order moves through states. The design must say which changes are allowed: it can be cancelled while placed or paid, but not after the kitchen starts. LLD also defines table columns and types, plus an index on (user_id, created_at) for “my orders.” It decides what to do if the payment call times out or the same order arrives twice.
steps.callout: Many production bugs come from an unhandled state change, a missing index, or a retry that charges twice.

steps.title: Contracts connect the two levels
body: HLD defines what a service promises at its edge: its API and the events it publishes. LLD decides how the service keeps that promise. This lets teams change code inside the service as long as POST /orders and OrderPlaced keep the same meaning.
steps.callout: Changing a contract affects other teams. Old and new versions may need to work side by side for a while. See API versioning.

steps.title: Design from the outside in
body: In an interview, one candidate may spend 20 minutes on class diagrams and never mention that courier locations arrive 40,000 times a second. Another may draw clear service boxes but not explain how an order avoids a double charge. Work top-down: clarify requirements, estimate the load, outline the API and data, draw the HLD, then examine the few hardest parts in more detail.
steps.callout: A design session often follows: requirements → estimates → API → data model → HLD → deep dives → failure cases. The next walkthroughs use this order.

steps.title: Recap
body:
HLDLLD
ViewWhole systemOne component
PartsServices, stores, queuesClasses, tables, states
DecidesConnections and data locationsHow each part works inside
ChangesLess often, with agreementOften, within a team
This course focuses on HLD and looks inside a component when a decision depends on it. LLD, including object-oriented design and design patterns, is a subject of its own.
